newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG confirms mercenaries to go to Bougainville.
newsitem.headline: PNG confirms mercenaries to go to Bougainville.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Tuesday admitted his government had hired mercenaries to accompany local troops on a mission against secessionist rebels on Bougainville -- but only as advisors.
"They would be taken in only as an advisory team, but we would not use them in the frontline," Chan told reporters in Port Moresby.
"We are no fools. We are a government, and no government would allow their citizens to be killed by foreigners," he said.
Meanwhile, hospitals in northern Australia were put on alert for casualties from any increase in the fighting on Bougainville island. Papua New Guinea is Australia's closest neighbour.

Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Tuesday that Papua New Guinea had planned a mercenary strike against the secessionist rebels on Bougainville, contradicting assurances by the South Pacific nation that it would not use foreign fighters.
Howard told a meeting of government MPs that he became aware last week of a plan to use mercenaries in the nine-year-old conflict on Bougainville.

"He (Howard) said it's obviously a very serious situation, (and) that he became aware last week that a mercenary strike against Bougainville rebels was planned," a government spokesman told reporters after the meeting.

On Monday, Papua New Guinea said it had no plans to use mercenaries to fight on Bougainville but had hired Sandlines International, a private military training and logistical group, to help train government soldiers fighting there.
"Yes there is training going on at the moment... I am sick and tired of our boys coming back in body bags," Chan said then.
Sandlines International is a subsidiary of British-registered Executive Outcomes, Africa's best known private army and which has helped Angola and Sierra Leone fight rebel threats.
But on Tuesday, Chan told reporters in Port Moresby that 40 military advisors were now training troops and would be part of a mission to Bougainville targetting rebel leaders.
"They are out here to build up the capabilities of our defence force," said Chan, adding that the decision to use mercenaries was taken 18 months ago.
Asked if armed advisors on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby, could be described as mercenaries, Chan said: "I suppose if you stretch it to the limit, it can."
He said the current operation, aimed at ending the rebellion would last a year and cost around A$36 million (US$27 million).
Chan said on Monday the option of using non-government soldiers to help train his military had been canvassed in a defence paper drawn up in consultation with Australia.
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer rejected this.

"Australia was not advised by PNG of its intention to hire mercenary forces," Downer told parliament on Tuesday. "The Department of Defence has not suggested at any stage that mercenaries have a role to play in PNG'security."

A bi-partisan motion lodged in the Australian parliament on Tuesday condemned the mercenary plan. The motion, to be debated next month, urged Australia to warn Papua New Guinea that the use of mercenaries would "prejudice our bilateral relationship".
Hundreds of people have died from the fighting or disease due to a lack of medical supplies in the Bougainville rebellion.
